title: The Missing Coefficients: Bayesian Pairwise Merging for Model Personalization

paper.title: The Missing Coefficients: Bayesian Pairwise Merging for Model Personalization
paper.abstract:
Abstract How can we personalize a shared expert library from a user’s pairwise choices?
Prior work can realize different reward trade-offs by merging reward-specialized experts, given a vector of trade-off weights.
In practice, users can more naturally choose between outputs than specify numerical weights.
The challenge is therefore to turn these choices into the coefficients required for merging, while accounting for ambiguity when feedback is limited.
Our key idea is to treat the unknown reward weights as latent variables: infer a posterior over them from pairwise choices and reward-score differences, and use its mean directly as the merge coefficients.
We instantiate this idea as Bayesian Pairwise Merging ( bpm ), whose posterior also characterizes which reward trade-offs remain plausible given the feedback.
We evaluate bpm on radiology summarization, image captioning, and story generation, spanning text-to-text and image-to-text generation.
With 100 feedback per simulated persona, bpm achieves macro decided win rates of 91.7%, 77.1%, and 64.3% against uniform merge.
For six pairs of simulated personas, each prefers the model fitted to its own feedback, a pattern also observed in a human proof-of-concept.
In simulations under bpm ’s model and prior, its nominal 90 % 90\% intervals for temperature-scaled reward weights achieve task-averaged marginal coverage of 88.9 % 88.9\% and 89.2 % 89.2\% with only 10 10 and 25 25 comparisons, respectively. bpm thus enables personalization from pairwise feedback without per-user policy training, while characterizing the coefficient ambiguity left by limited feedback.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Personalizing generative models requires adapting to how users trade off competing objectives ( Guan et al., 2025 ; Ji et al., 2026 ) . Existing multi-objective methods can realize different trade-offs once a preference vector is given ( Zhong et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . A representative example is Rewarded Soups ( Rame et al., 2023 ) , which merges reward-specialized experts with different coefficients to construct models for different preferences. The same expert library can then be reused across users, avoiding a separate training run for every trade-off. These methods assume that the preference weights are already known. Users, however, may find it easier to compare generated outputs than to specify numerical weights over reward dimensions. The central question is how a user’s pairwise choices can supply the missing coefficients for model personalization . Answering this question requires connecting preference inference with model construction. Prior work has shown that pairwise choices can inform estimates of user-specific reward weights ( Bose et al., 2025 ) , but limited feedback may leave multiple weight vectors plausible ( Shenfeld et al., 2025 ) . Yet even accurate reward-weight estimates do not guarantee the intended trade-offs in the merged model ( Rame et al., 2023 , §2.2.3) . Thus, translating uncertain preference estimates into effective merge coefficients remains a challenge. Figure 1: Pairwise feedback personalizes a merged model. Two simulated personas provide different choices (a) , inducing distinct posteriors (b) and merged-model outputs (c) . Each persona favors its corresponding model on shared response pairs (d) . In this work, we propose Bayesian Pairwise Merging ( bpm ) , which connects uncertain preference inference with the construction of a personalized model ( Figure 1 ). To account for the ambiguity left by limited feedback, bpm uses Bayesian inference to obtain a posterior over user-specific reward weights, quantifying the relative support for different trade-offs and the uncertainty that remains. The posterior mean then supplies the coefficients for merging shared reward-specialized experts, enabling classical Bayesian inference to guide the personalization of modern deep generative models without per-user policy training. Our theoretical analysis makes explicit the additional assumptions needed to connect accurate weight estimation with optimality. Experiments on radiology summarization ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , image captioning ( Chen et al., 2015 ) , and story generation ( Fan et al., 2018 ) demonstrate effective personalization and characterize the stability and uncertainty of the inferred coefficients. Our main contributions are threefold. 1. Pairwise feedback supplies effective model-construction coefficients. bpm connects Bayesian reward-weight inference to shared-expert merging, constructing personalized models without explicit user-specified weights or per-user policy training. The inferred coefficients improve on uniform merging across three generation tasks, establishing a practical route from pairwise choices to personalized models (§ 3 and § 5.1 ). 2. Inferred coefficients translate preference differences into model behavior. Across three generation tasks, simulated personas favor models fitted to their own feedback, and controlled changes in feedback preferences produce corresponding behavioral shifts. Together, these findings demonstrate preference following beyond aggregate improvements in model performance (§ 5.2 ). 3. bpm stabilizes coefficients and quantifies uncertainty. bpm ’s posterior means vary less than mle coefficients across feedback subsets at n ≤ 100 n\leq 100 in all three tasks. In simulations under bpm ’s model and prior, compact intervals for temperature-scaled reward weights achieve near-nominal coverage. bpm thus provides reduced coefficient sensitivity and quantified reward-weight ambiguity, complementing output preference as distinct dimensions of personalization (§ 6 , Appendix F ).

sections.heading: Multi-objective alignment with specified preferences.
sections.text: Given a preference vector, existing methods implement the corresponding trade-offs through weighted-reward optimization ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , preference-conditioned policies ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2024a ) , decoding-time composition ( Shi et al., 2024 ) , or preference-aware model merging ( Rame et al., 2023 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Chen and Kwok, 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Related work on multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrates specialized teachers into a student through additional training ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . bpm addresses how to obtain the preference weights themselves from an individual’s pairwise choices, then uses them to merge shared experts without per-user policy training.

sections.heading: Preference inference from pairwise feedback.
sections.text: Prior work learns reward functions from human comparisons ( Christiano et al., 2017 ) and uses Bayesian inference to estimate reward weights as well as their uncertainty ( Biyik and Sadigh, 2018 ; Bıyık et al., 2020 ) . PReF ( Shenfeld et al., 2025 ) and LoRe ( Bose et al., 2025 ) infer user-specific weights over reward components learned across users, while other methods model preference distributions ( Poddar et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . bpm uses predefined reward dimensions without requiring other users’ preference data. In connecting feedback to personalized outputs, UserAlign selects responses from a fixed candidate pool ( Pădurean et al., 2025 ) , while Spectral Souping estimates policy-combination coefficients from online feedback, including through sequential Gaussian posterior updates ( Chow et al., 2026 ) . bpm infers a posterior over reward weights from a fixed offline set of pairwise judgments.

sections.heading: 3 Bayesian Pairwise Merging
sections.text: Figure 2: Bayesian Pairwise Merging. A persona’s pairwise feedback updates a shared prior over reward weights into a posterior, whose mean supplies the merge coefficients and whose spread quantifies their uncertainty. Norm. denotes normalization by the infinity norm. Bayesian pairwise merging (BPM) personalizes a model for each persona , which represents an individual or a group of users with shared preferences. From pairwise feedback, bpm constructs a personalized model and characterizes uncertainty in the inferred reward weights. Figure 2 and Algorithm 1 summarize the procedure, with key notations listed in Table 3 .

sections.heading: Tasks and datasets.
sections.text: We evaluate bpm on three tasks spanning text-only and vision-language settings. For Summarization , models generate a short impression from the comprehensive radiology report findings in the MIMIC-CXR dataset ( Johnson et al., 2024 ) . For Image Captioning , models use free-form text to describe images from COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . For Story Generation , models write short stories in response to instructions from Writing Prompts ( Fan et al., 2018 ) .

sections.heading: Expert libraries.
sections.text: For each task, we use standard evaluation metrics as reward dimensions, scored by computed metrics or an LLM scorer (gpt-oss-20b) separate from the persona judges, and train one LoRA expert ( Hu et al., 2022 ) per dimension from a shared base model using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . The libraries comprise 29 29 reward-specialized experts based on Qwen3.5-2B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) for radiology report summarization, 21 21 on Qwen3-VL-4B ( Bai et al., 2025 ) for image captioning, and 16 16 on Ministral-3-3B ( Liu et al., 2026a ) for story generation. To assess bpm ’s robustness to variations in training, we construct additional Summarization libraries using GRPO with two more seeds, RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , or DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . All libraries are shared across personas, with persona-specific feedback determining the merge coefficients. Reward definitions and training details are provided in Appendices B.2 and B.3 , respectively.

sections.heading: Persona simulation.
sections.text: We simulate personas through either natural-language descriptions or explicit weights over rubric criteria. For prompt-based personas , we use Qwen3.5-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) to simulate six personas for Summarization and seven for Story Generation , while for Image Captioning , six personas are simulated with Qwen3-VL-32B ( Team, 2025 ) . Both models are conditioned on system prompts describing diverse preferences, including those not explicitly represented by the reward library (Appendix C ). For rubric-based personas , we construct five for Story Generation using AutoRubric ( Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026 ) for weighted rubric evaluation, with adjustable criterion weights specifying preferences. These weights remain hidden from bpm and can be varied to study how personalized models follow changes in preference (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Preference assignment.
sections.text: Prompt-based personas use the same LLM and persona description to provide pairwise feedback and evaluate model outputs on disjoint test inputs. Each response pair is judged in both presentation orders; feedback collection retains only valid, non-tied choices that agree across orders. Rubric-based personas assign preferences according to persona-weighted rubric scores, with tied or invalid comparisons excluded from feedback. The feedback budget n n counts retained comparisons rather than individual judge queries.

sections.heading: Compared methods.
sections.text: We compare bpm with methods that personalize through expert weighting ( rm and l2w ), response selection ( bt-bon ), prompting ( icai ), or policy training ( dpo ), alongside the base policy and uniform merge ( rs ). For each persona and budget, methods that use pairwise feedback receive the same sampled subsets as bpm . • Uniform merge ( rs ) uses the equal-weight configuration of Rewarded Soups ( Rame et al., 2023 ) , 𝜽 ⁡ ( 𝟏 / L ) \bm{\theta}(\mathbf{1}/L) , which is also bpm ’s policy before observing persona-specific pairwise feedback. And • base policy is the shared base model 𝜽 0 \bm{\theta}_{0} before reward-specific expert training. • Ridge merge ( rm ) fits an unconstrained coefficient vector with ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularized logistic regression and maps it to the simplex through a softmax, returning a penalized point estimate in place of bpm ’s posterior, which represents the point-estimate preference recovery of PReF ( Shenfeld et al., 2025 ) and LoRe ( Bose et al., 2025 ) , adapted to our merge family. • Maximum likelihood and maximum a posteriori merging ( mle / map ) fit the same Bradley–Terry preference model as bpm . mle omits the priors, whereas map uses the joint posterior mode in transformed coordinates, including the transformation Jacobian (Appendix F ). • Adapted Spectral Souping ( ss-a ) uses the coefficient estimator of Chow et al. (2026) with the same offline preference pairs, replacing policy-derived features with standardized reward-score differences. It fits signed coefficients under an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} constraint and uses exact delta merging to accommodate negative coefficients (Appendix G ). • Preference-based reranking ( bt-bon ) fits a Bradley-Terry reward model to the preference pairs and selects the highest-scoring output among eight samples from the uniform merge ( Nakano et al., 2022 ; Gui et al., 2024 ) , which applies personalization through output selection. • Language-to-Weights ( l2w ) follows the language-guided weighting approach of Promptable Behaviors ( Hwang et al., 2024 ) , using gpt-oss-20b ( OpenAI, 2025 ) to infer reward weights from the persona description, which is not provided to bpm . The inferred weights are normalized and used as merge coefficients. • Inverse Constitutional AI ( icai ) uses gpt-oss-20b to infer a constitution from the preference pairs, following Findeis et al. (2025) . The same constitution is supplied as a system prompt to either the base policy icai-b , as in the original setting, or the uniform merge icai-m , bpm ’s starting policy. • Direct preference optimization ( dpo ) fine-tunes the base policy on each persona’s preference pairs ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) , requiring per-persona training that bpm avoids by merging shared experts. This compared method is distinct from the DPO-trained expert libraries described above. Further details on compared method configurations, training budgets, and hyperparameter selection are provided in Appendix B.5 .

sections.heading: Test evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate on 451 451 radiology reports, 500 500 images, and 500 500 story prompts with the same two-order judgment protocol. Decided win rates are N win / ( N win + N loss ) N_{\mathrm{win}}/(N_{\mathrm{win}}+N_{\mathrm{loss}}) ; supplementary scores retain valid ties and order-inconsistent judgments at half credit, with assignment sensitivity reported in Appendix G.1 . Macro rates equally weight personas and average over feedback draws. The 95% input-bootstrap intervals condition on the observed personas, feedback subsets, and expert library (Appendix B.7 ).

sections.heading: Effectiveness of feedback-derived coefficients.
sections.text: bpm improves on uniform merging across all three tasks at both feedback budgets ( Table 1 ), showing that pairwise feedback supplies useful coefficients for personalizing the shared expert library. On Story Generation , gains over uniform merging also persist with gpt-oss-20 as an alternative judge ( Figure 3 e).

sections.heading: Comparison with alternative methods.
sections.text: bpm outperforms ridge merge and preference-based reranking, whereas mle and adapted ss often yield more preferred outputs, and comparisons with map vary by task and budget. The lower block compares methods that use an auxiliary LLM for personalization or require per-persona policy training, § 6 § 6 examines what bpm ’s posterior additionally provides in terms of coefficient stability and uncertainty.

sections.heading: Limited feedback supports personalization.
sections.text: Figure 3 c shows gains over uniform merge with as few as 10 10 comparisons in all three tasks, demonstrating that even a small number of choices can supply useful coefficients. These gains generally increase with the feedback budget, supporting personalization from limited feedback and further improvement as more choices become available. sections.heading: bpm reflects persona-specific preferences.
sections.text: To assess whether inferred weights translate feedback into preference-specific model behavior, we select two simulated persona pairs per task and have both personas judge the same outputs from their respective models. Each persona favors its own model in all six pairs ( Figure 3 a). A single author-annotator also exhibits preference reversals under the Picture Book (PB) and Magazine Editor (ME descriptions in a human proof-of-concept (Appendix E.2 ). Length- and readability-matched analyses appear in Appendix E.3 .

sections.heading: bpm follows controlled preference shifts.
sections.text: Rubric-based personas allow us to vary feedback preferences while keeping the evaluation criteria fixed. As shown in Table 2 b, bpm retains its macro advantage over the compared methods on the task of story generation. As feedback shifts from Literary toward Genre , win rates against uniform decrease under the fixed Literary judge and increase overall under the fixed Genre judge ( Figure 3 b), supporting the responsiveness of the merged models to changes in pairwise feedback preferences.

sections.heading: Posterior means reduce coefficient variation under limited feedback.
sections.text: To assess sensitivity to feedback sampling, we measure the mean pairwise ℓ 1 \ell_{1} distance between coefficients fitted to three feedback subsets, averaged over personas. Figure 4 a shows lower variation for bpm than mle at n ≤ 100 n\leq 100 in all three tasks. Compared with adapted ss , the advantage holds across tasks at n = 10 n=10 , with task-dependent differences at larger budgets. Appendix F.3 reports paired intervals.

sections.heading: Coefficient stability and output preference are distinct.
sections.text: bpm improves on uniform merging while reducing coefficient variation relative to mle under limited feedback. This stability advantage does not imply higher output preference: mle and adapted ss often yield more preferred outputs. Conversely, rm can be more stable than bpm but is less preferred at both main-table budgets. bpm thus provides useful personalization with greater stability under limited feedback and a posterior over plausible weights, rather than a uniformly superior stability–preference trade-off (Appendix F.3 ).

sections.heading: bpm quantifies support for alternative reward trade-offs.
sections.text: Starting from a shared prior, the Literary and Librarian posteriors favor stylistically rich expression and clear, accessible storytelling, respectively (Appendix F.1 ). Their means supply persona-specific merge coefficients, while the full posteriors quantify the relative support for alternative reward trade-offs under the model and prior. bpm thus provides both a concrete personalization choice and a probabilistic account of which alternatives remain plausible given the feedback.

sections.heading: bpm provides compact intervals with near-nominal coverage in matched simulations.
sections.text: In simulations under bpm ’s model and prior, nominal 90% intervals for 𝜷 = 𝐰 / τ \bm{\beta}=\mathbf{w}/\tau achieve coverage of 88.9% and 89.2% after 10 and 25 comparisons ( Figure 3 d). map , mle , and rm bootstrap intervals under-cover, whereas rm Laplace and ss Gaussian intervals are substantially wider and approach full coverage. Prior-only intervals have comparable coverage and widths, and prior perturbations reduce coverage in some settings (Appendix F.2 ). bpm thus provides compact uncertainty summaries with near-nominal coverage under the assumed model and prior, with limited evidence of interval contraction at these budgets.

sections.heading: Posterior uncertainty contextualizes personalization performance.
sections.text: To relate uncertainty to model behavior, Figure 4 b compares U U with win rates across personas within each task and budget. Lower uncertainty is associated with higher win rates, while the association is weak on Story Generation . bpm thus complements preference scores by quantifying the coefficient ambiguity remaining for each persona (Appendix F.1 ). sections.heading: Posteriors reveal persona-specific reward trade-offs.
sections.text: To examine how feedback updates the shared prior, Figure 6 shows six reward-weight marginals for two personas on Story Generation at n = 500 n=500 . The Literary posterior favors expressive writing, whereas the Librarian posterior favors clear, coherent storytelling. Beyond supplying merge coefficients through posterior means, bpm quantifies support for alternative weight values under the model and prior.

sections.heading: Gains persist across expert libraries.
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 a, bpm outperforms each library’s own uniform merge with both RLOO- and DPO-trained experts on Summarization . The gains hold for every persona at both feedback budgets, supporting feedback-based personalization of expert libraries trained with different optimization methods.

sections.heading: Inferred weights support policy training.
sections.text: Using inferred Ward and Emergency Doctor (ED) weights yields Summarization policies preferred over uniform-weight training and training with the other persona’s weights (Appendix E.5 ), extending the usefulness of bpm ’s inferred weights beyond model merging.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We present bpm , which obtains the missing coefficients for model personalization by inferring a posterior over reward weights from pairwise choices and using its mean to merge shared experts, without per-user policy training. Across three generation tasks, the resulting models improve on uniform merging and reflect contrasting simulated persona preferences, while controlled feedback shifts produce corresponding behavioral changes. Gains across expert libraries trained with different optimization methods further support the usefulness of feedback-derived coefficients. Beyond model construction, bpm provides coefficients that vary less than mle across limited-feedback subsets and a posterior quantifying plausible reward weights. In simulations under its model and prior, compact intervals for temperature-scaled reward weights achieve near-nominal coverage. bpm thus connects pairwise feedback to personalized models while making the remaining ambiguity in the inferred preferences explicit.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with experimental design, method implementation, and mathematical derivations. LLMs were also used to simulate personas to provide pairwise preference judgments and evaluate generated outputs, as documented in the experimental setup and appendix. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to assist with literature discovery, manuscript organization, drafting, and language editing. All AI-assisted work was reviewed by the authors. AI-generated code was checked and tested by at least one author, and the manuscript was proofread by all authors. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including its text, mathematical claims, experimental results, and AI-assisted artifacts.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This research involves human annotations to construct pairwise feedback. All annotation tasks were conducted by the authors of this paper, who participated voluntarily and with full knowledge of the study’s purpose, procedures, and intended use of the data. No external crowdsourcing or paid annotation platforms were employed. The study does not involve sensitive personal data, human subjects outside of the annotation task, or applications that raise privacy, security, or legal concerns. We also follow the standard research ethics protocols of our institution, with explicit approval from the IRB, for all internal annotation efforts. The research complies with the ICLR Code of Ethics, and no conflicts of interest or sponsorship concerns are associated with this work.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: The main paper and appendix describe the components needed to reproduce bpm , including reward normalization, prior specification, posterior inference, and model merging, together with datasets and splits, expert training configurations, persona prompts, feedback collection procedures, and evaluation protocols. We also document the compared methods’ configuration, simulation settings, and confidence interval estimation procedures. The supplementary code provides a synthetic inference demo and core pipeline components. We will release the full implementation and experiment configurations to support reproducibility and future research. These efforts are intended to enable the community to replicate our experiments and build upon our findings.

sections.heading: Appendix C Persona Specifications
sections.text: The following descriptions and comparison instructions define the six, six, and seven main personas for Summarization , Image Captioning , and Story Generation , respectively, and remain fixed between pool simulation and test evaluation. The additional captioning persona Annotator is used only in diagnostic analyses and is excluded from the main macro averages.

sections.heading: Common instruction.
sections.text: The IMPRESSION section is a summary written from the FINDINGS section. You are judging two candidate impressions produced from the same findings. The persona description below defines the intended use and the trade-offs you should apply. Apply those criteria consistently regardless of whether a candidate is labelled A or B.

sections.heading: Default instruction.
sections.text: The IMPRESSION section of a radiology report is a summary of the FINDINGS section: it must convey the clinically important content of the findings without restating them in full. You are a radiologist judging two candidate summaries of the same findings.

sections.heading: Comparison template.
sections.text: FINDINGS: {source} SUMMARY A: {a} SUMMARY B: {b} Which is the better summary of these findings under your stated criteria? Choose TIE only if the two are effectively equivalent under those criteria; otherwise choose one even if the difference is small. Do not restate the candidate summaries in your reasoning. Give at most two sentences of reasoning, then end with a line of exactly this form: VERDICT: A (or) VERDICT: B (or) VERDICT: TIE

sections.heading: Ward.
sections.text: You are the ward clinician who will act on this impression. Check each summary against the findings for what it omits: new or changed findings, support devices and their position, and relevant negatives that affect inpatient management. Prefer the summary that omits less of that content; missing information is worse than extra length. Reject any diagnosis the findings do not support, however plausible. When both cover the management-relevant content, brevity is welcome.

sections.heading: ED.
sections.text: You are the emergency clinician reading this impression during a busy shift. You want the single most urgent, actionable conclusion stated first and as briefly as possible. Whenever both summaries state the urgent conclusion, prefer the shorter one; every extra sentence costs you reading time. A summary that buries or omits the urgent finding is seriously flawed, as is one that asserts an unsupported diagnosis. Detail that would not change acute management is a cost rather than a benefit.

sections.heading: Complete.
sections.text: You judge a summary by how much of the report’s clinically relevant content it retains, including negative and incidental findings. A summary that drops a relevant finding has failed, even if it is short and reads well. Length is not a fault.

sections.heading: Concise.
sections.text: You judge a summary by how concisely it states the key diagnosis. A summary that restates findings or adds anything beyond the main conclusion has not summarised, however accurate it is. Omitting minor findings is not a fault.

sections.heading: Faithful.
sections.text: You judge a summary by whether every statement in it is supported by the findings. Any claim, diagnosis or inference that the findings do not state is a failure, however plausible. Length and completeness are not what you judge.

sections.heading: Calibrated.
sections.text: You judge a summary by whether it preserves the certainty level of the findings: possible or probable findings must stay qualified, definite ones stated as such. Overstated certainty is a failure. Length and completeness are not what you judge.

sections.heading: Common instruction.
sections.text: You are judging two one-sentence captions written for the same photograph, which you can see. The persona description below defines the intended use and the trade-offs you should apply. Apply those criteria consistently regardless of whether a candidate is labelled A or B.

sections.heading: Default instruction.
sections.text: A caption is a single-sentence description of an image, written for someone who cannot see it. You are looking at the image and judging two candidate captions of it.

sections.heading: Comparison template.
sections.text: CAPTION A: {a} CAPTION B: {b} Which is the better caption for this image under your stated criteria? Choose TIE only if the two are effectively equivalent under those criteria; otherwise choose one even if the difference is small. Do not restate the candidate captions in your reasoning. Give at most two sentences of reasoning, then end with a line of exactly this form: VERDICT: A (or) VERDICT: B (or) VERDICT: TIE

sections.heading: Default.
sections.text: No additional persona description is supplied; the default instruction above is used.

sections.heading: Indexer.
sections.text: You catalogue images for visual search. You prefer the caption that specifically names more of the objects that are visible. When attributes, colours, and counts are clear, you want them included. You also value the setting when it would help someone retrieve the image. You treat every omission of something clearly visible as a fault, but you do not penalize a caption for being long.

sections.heading: Magazine Editor.
sections.text: You edit a photography magazine and appreciate fine prose. You prefer a caption that forms a well-crafted sentence with vivid, precise, and varied vocabulary. You value an evocative sense of light, texture, and atmosphere, along with graceful rhythm. You treat plain, inventory-like wording as a fault. You welcome length when every word earns its place. You still require the caption to describe this image rather than a different one.

sections.heading: Verifier.
sections.text: You edit captions before publication and prefer the caption whose every statement is directly supported by what you can see. You treat claims about people’s feelings or intentions, the scene’s location, events before or after the pictured moment, and anything outside the frame as faults, however plausible they seem. You also penalize any object, colour, or count that is not shown. You do not judge coverage, length, or style.

sections.heading: Picture Book.
sections.text: You choose captions for a picture book aimed at young children. You prefer one complete sentence that a six-year-old can read aloud and understand. It uses common everyday words, stays short and concrete, and says what is happening. You treat rare or long words, sub-clauses, lists, and abstract language as faults. You do not penalize a caption for leaving out minor details in the background.

sections.heading: Alt-text.
sections.text: You write alt text for someone using a screen reader. You prefer one short, plain sentence that identifies the main subject, describes its most important visible action, and includes only the context needed to understand the image. You penalize speculation, decorative language, and background details that do not change the meaning. You consider a caption unsuccessful if it omits the main subject or its action.

sections.heading: Annotator (additional diagnostic persona).
sections.text: Excluded from the main macro averages. You annotate images for a COCO-style captioning dataset and follow its annotation guidelines. You prefer one plain sentence of roughly eight to fifteen words that names the important objects, says what they are doing, uses ordinary words, and avoids proper names. You treat guesses about the past, the future, feelings, or anything outside the frame as faults, along with decorative wording and minor background details. You do not penalize a longer or rarer word when it is the accurate one.

sections.heading: Common instruction.
sections.text: You are shown a writing prompt and two stories written in response to it. The persona description below defines the role you read in and the trade-offs you should apply. Apply those criteria consistently regardless of whether a story is labelled A or B.

sections.heading: Default instruction.
sections.text: You are shown a writing prompt and two stories written in response to it.

sections.heading: Comparison template.
sections.text: WRITING PROMPT: {source} STORY A: {a} STORY B: {b} Which story would you, in this role, rather publish or read? Choose TIE only if the two are effectively equivalent under your stated criteria; otherwise choose one even if the difference is small. Do not restate the stories in your reasoning. Give at most two sentences of reasoning, then end with a line of exactly this form: VERDICT: A (or) VERDICT: B (or) VERDICT: TIE

sections.heading: Literary.
sections.text: You are the fiction editor of a literary magazine. You value restraint and precision: concrete images that do the emotional work, characters revealed through what they do and notice rather than through statements about how they feel, and endings that trust the reader. Clichés, melodrama, decoration without purpose, and sentences that explain what the story has already shown all count against a story. Extra length earns no credit by itself, and you would rather publish a restrained, emotionally suggestive story with little action than a brisk, neatly resolved one whose prose is less precise.

sections.heading: Genre.
sections.text: You are an acquiring editor for a commercial genre imprint (thriller, fantasy, science fiction, romance). You want a story that hooks in the first lines, makes the central problem clear, moves through consequential action and dialogue, and resolves that problem with an earned payoff. You prefer forward action and a clear resolution to sustained interior reflection and an ending left open to interpretation. You would rather acquire a brisk, clearly resolved story in plain, serviceable prose than a beautifully phrased, reflective one with little forward action.

sections.heading: Librarian.
sections.text: You are a children’s librarian choosing stories to read aloud to six- to nine-year-olds. You want clear, mostly familiar language that reads naturally aloud, sympathetic characters a child can root for, and a warm, reassuring ending. Frightening or adult material and persistently difficult wording count strongly against a story, while brief, understandable moments of danger or sadness can work within a reassuring whole.

sections.heading: Flash.
sections.text: You judge flash fiction and prefer compact stories, usually around 300 words or fewer. You favour a tightly focused situation, a memorable central image, and an ending that changes how the reader sees what came before. You value compression, but a slightly longer story can win when its extra words make the image or the final turn more effective.

sections.heading: Screenwriter.
sections.text: You are a screenwriter who enjoys short fiction built around dramatic scenes. You favour concrete scenes where distinctive dialogue and visible action reveal conflict and character, with thoughts and backstory kept brief. You prefer conflict enacted between characters to extended interior monologue or descriptive passages that interrupt a scene.

sections.heading: Restorative.
sections.text: You read fiction from a restorative perspective on wrongdoing. When a story deals with harm, you favour one that treats accountability as repair — the wrongdoer understanding what they did, the harmed person having a say, some restoration attempted, however partial — over one that resolves through punishment, revenge, or the wrongdoer simply getting what was coming to them. This holds even when the punitive story is equally coherent, equally moving, and equally well written. Where a story involves no wrongdoing, judge it on whether it takes its human situation seriously.

sections.heading: Default.
sections.text: No additional persona description is supplied; the default instruction above is used.

sections.heading: D.1 Criterion Definitions and Score Anchors
sections.text: The following four-level anchors specify the story-quality criteria. For positively oriented criteria, reward is the level divided by three. For fault criteria, reward is one minus the level divided by three. The same definitions and anchors are supplied to the reward scorer and the persona criterion scorer.

sections.heading: relevance.
sections.text: How well the story matches the writing prompt. 0. The story ignores the prompt: none of the prompt’s premise, characters or situation appears in it. 1. The story touches the prompt only loosely, picking up a word or a mood but not the situation the prompt sets up. 2. The story clearly works from the prompt but drops or contradicts part of its premise. 3. The story takes on the prompt’s whole premise and stays inside it from beginning to end.

sections.heading: coherence.
sections.text: How much the story makes sense. 0. The story does not make sense: sentences do not connect, or characters and events change without explanation. 1. Individual passages read, but the story as a whole is confusing, with events or characters that contradict each other. 2. The story mostly follows, with one or two jumps, loose ends or inconsistencies a reader has to work around. 3. Every event and character follows from what came before; nothing in the story has to be explained away.

sections.heading: empathy.
sections.text: How well the reader understood the characters’ emotions. 0. The characters have no discernible emotional life; there is nothing for the reader to understand. 1. Emotions are only asserted or named, so the reader is told how a character feels without being able to feel it. 2. The reader understands what the characters feel at the story’s main turns, though not consistently. 3. The reader follows the characters’ feelings throughout, grounded in what the characters do, say and notice.

sections.heading: surprise.
sections.text: How surprising the end of the story was. 0. The ending is entirely predictable, or the story simply stops without arriving anywhere. 1. The ending is the obvious continuation of the premise, with nothing the reader had not already assumed. 2. The ending contains a turn the reader did not expect, though a mild or familiar one. 3. The ending genuinely surprises and still fits the story, changing how the reader sees what came before.

sections.heading: engagement.
sections.text: How much the reader engaged with the story. 0. The story gives the reader no reason to continue; reading it is an effort. 1. The story holds attention in places but stalls, repeats itself or loses the reader’s interest. 2. The story keeps the reader reading, though attention slackens in parts of it. 3. The story holds the reader from the first lines to the last and makes them want to know what happens.

sections.heading: complexity.
sections.text: How elaborate the story is. 0. The story is a bare sketch: one flat situation, no development of character, plot or theme. 1. The story has a simple single thread with little development beyond stating what happens. 2. The story develops a plot, a character or an idea with some depth, but along a single dimension. 3. The story is elaborate, developing plot, characters and theme together and holding them in relation.

sections.heading: Imagery & Descriptive Quality.
sections.text: How vividly and concretely the story renders what can be seen, heard, touched, smelled and tasted. 0. The story is abstract throughout: nothing in it can be pictured, and no sense beyond sight is engaged even in outline. 1. Description is generic – rooms, faces and weather named but not rendered, with images that could belong to any story. 2. The story contains some concrete, specific images that a reader can see, though much of it stays at the level of summary. 3. The story is rendered in precise, particular sensory detail that puts the reader in the scene, with images chosen rather than defaulted to.

sections.heading: Elegant Prose.
sections.text: How well-made the sentences are: rhythm, control of syntax, word choice, and variation. 0. The prose is clumsy: broken or monotonous syntax, repeated sentence shapes, and words that do not mean what the sentence needs. 1. The prose is serviceable but flat – correct sentences with no rhythm, no variation in length or shape, and predictable diction. 2. The prose is controlled and readable, with some variation of rhythm and some well-chosen words, but also passages that go slack. 3. The prose is consistently well made: sentences vary in shape and rhythm to a purpose, and the diction is precise throughout.

sections.heading: Tell-Don’t-Show.
sections.text: How much the story states its content outright instead of dramatising it. This is a FAULT: score how badly the story tells rather than shows. 0. The story dramatises throughout: what characters feel and what is at stake reaches the reader through action, speech and detail. 1. The story mostly dramatises, with one or two places where it stops to state outright something it has already shown. 2. The story tells often – feelings, motives and significance are announced to the reader as much as they are enacted. 3. The story is told rather than dramatised: it is a report of what happened and what it meant, with little or nothing enacted on the page.

sections.heading: Purple Prose.
sections.text: How overwrought the writing is: ornamental adjectives, strained metaphor, and grandiosity out of proportion to the material. This is a FAULT: score how purple the prose is. 0. The writing is unadorned; every image and modifier earns its place. 1. There are occasional ornamental flourishes or an over-reached metaphor, but the prose is not carried away. 2. The writing is frequently overwrought: stacked adjectives, strained figures and a register grander than the material. 3. The writing is relentlessly purple – ornament substitutes for substance and the prose is exhausting to read.

sections.heading: Weak Dialogue.
sections.text: How poorly the spoken lines work: stiff or interchangeable voices, exposition delivered as speech, and dialogue that does no work in the scene. This is a FAULT: score how weak the dialogue is. A story with no dialogue at all cannot be strong on this criterion and is scored 2. 0. The dialogue is alive: distinct voices, lines that carry the scene, and nothing said only for the reader’s benefit. 1. The dialogue mostly works, with a few stiff lines or a passage where a character explains something for the reader. 2. The dialogue is weak: voices are interchangeable, lines are stilted, or speech is used chiefly to deliver exposition. A story with no dialogue is scored here. 3. The dialogue is unusable – wooden, uniform and purely expository – or the story is one where speech was needed and none of it convinces.

sections.heading: Persona-specific posterior distributions.
sections.text: To illustrate what bpm provides beyond a single coefficient vector, we compare the shared prior with the reward-weight posteriors for the Literary and Librarian personas on Story Generation at n = 500 n=500 . Figure 6 shows six selected marginal distributions. The Literary posterior assigns greater weight to show-don’t-tell, prose elegance, and imagery, whereas the Librarian posterior emphasizes avoiding purple prose and coherence. The means supply coefficients for constructing the personalized models; the distributions additionally quantify support for alternative values of each weight under the model and prior. These examples illustrate persona-specific updates and the information retained by the posterior beyond the coefficients used for merging. Figure 6: Persona-specific reward-weight distributions. sections.heading: Uncertainty and personalization performance.
sections.text: For each persona and feedback budget, we average posterior uncertainty U U and the decided win rate against uniform merging separately over the three feedback subsets. We compute Spearman correlations between these averages within each task and budget, using six Summarization personas, six Image Captioning personas, and seven Story Generation personas. The six correlations in Figure 4 b therefore describe between-persona variation with task and budget held fixed. Lower uncertainty is associated with higher preference win rates in some task–budget setting, providing context for interpreting posterior uncertainty.

sections.heading: Calibration under the matched model and prior.
sections.text: We compare interval procedures on shared simulated feedback with a common target 𝜷 ⋆ = 𝐰 ⋆ / τ ⋆ \bm{\beta}^{\star}=\mathbf{w}^{\star}/\tau^{\star} . Generating weights and temperatures follow bpm ’s prior, and choices follow the Bradley–Terry likelihood on each task’s normalized contrasts. Coverage and width are averaged over coefficient coordinates and simulations within each task, then equally over tasks. Table 11 characterizes the tested procedures under this generating distribution; it does not establish calibration for observed persona preferences.

sections.heading: The prior contributes substantially at small budgets.
sections.text: Prior-only intervals attain near-nominal coverage and are slightly narrower on average than the posterior intervals at n = 10 n=10 and 25 25 . Thus, the matched comparison does not demonstrate interval contraction due to feedback. This does not imply that the posterior equals the prior: posterior location and shape can change without a decrease in average interval width. The 𝐰 \mathbf{w} marginals at n = 500 n=500 in Appendix F.1 illustrate persona-specific updates in a separate setting, while the stress tests assess sensitivity to generating and fitted assumptions.

sections.heading: Comparison with regularized estimation.
sections.text: We next examine whether regularized point estimation combined with standard interval constructions reproduces this behavior. We fit RM’s logistic estimator to the same normalized contrasts and construct bootstrap and Laplace intervals for its raw coefficient β \beta . This coefficient is unconstrained and regularized toward zero, whereas bpm constrains β = w / τ \beta=w/\tau through simplex weights. RM bootstrap intervals under-cover despite being wider than bpm ’s; Laplace intervals instead over-cover and are much wider ( Table 11 ). Thus, the two tested constructions do not reproduce bpm ’s interval performance in this simulation, illustrating that regularizing a point estimate alone does not determine the quality of its uncertainty estimates. sections.text: To examine the scope of these results, we vary the generating weights, the fitted prior, and the amount of label noise. Table 12 summarizes 16 settings across three tasks at n ∈ { 10 , 25 , 100 } n\in\{10,25,100\} , with 50 replicates per setting, task, and budget. Coverage of the simplex weights w w remains near nominal under the tested label-flip rates, but falls to 70.6 70.6 – 77.1 % 77.1\% when the fitted Dirichlet concentration is doubled. For generating weights concentrated on three dimensions, coverage on Story Generation falls to 81.1 81.1 – 81.4 % 81.4\% . Sensitivity also depends on the coefficient target: halving the standard deviation of the log ⁡ τ \log\tau prior yields 87.7 87.7 – 90.4 % 90.4\% coverage for w w , but 78.6 78.6 – 88.6 % 88.6\% for β \beta . Across the tested settings, mean posterior interval widths for w w are approximately 92 92 – 100 % 100\% of the corresponding prior widths. sections.heading: Inference and simulation details.
sections.text: The matched comparison uses 100 simulations per task and budget, with w ∼ Dir ⁡ ( s ​ 𝟏 ) w\sim\operatorname{Dir}(s\mathbf{1}) and log ⁡ τ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( log ⁡ 2 , 1 ) \log\tau\sim\mathcal{N}(\log 2,1) . bpm intervals are central posterior intervals; MAP and MLE intervals are percentile intervals from 200 bootstrap refits. Failed point-estimate fits are retried and then discarded; simulations without surviving refits count as noncoverage. SS uses the sequential Gaussian update of Chow et al. (2026), initialized with 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) and without the signed point estimator’s ℓ 1 \ell_{1} constraint; marginal intervals are the Gaussian mean plus or minus 1.645 1.645 marginal standard deviations. The iterated-update variant gives similar results. Prior intervals use 400,000 400{,}000 Monte Carlo draws. RM uses no intercept and a fixed ℓ 2 \ell_{2} penalty of one, with the same 200 bootstrap resamples as MAP and MLE. Its Laplace intervals are β ^ j ± 1.645 ​ ( H − 1 ) j ​ j \hat{\beta}_{j}\pm 1.645\sqrt{(H^{-1})_{jj}} , where H H is the Hessian of the penalized objective. For this comparison, RM is refitted on the shared ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} -normalized contrasts, rather than the pre-normalization standardized contrasts used in its model-personalization pipeline; its intervals concern raw logistic coefficients, not softmax weights. In the stress tests, the mass remaining after assigning one weight of 0.8 0.8 or three weights of 0.3 0.3 is shared equally among the other dimensions; near-uniform weights are drawn from Dir ⁡ ( 50 ​ 𝟏 ) \operatorname{Dir}(50\mathbf{1}) . Prior-sensitivity settings change only the stated fitted-prior parameter, and label-noise settings independently flip each simulated choice with the stated probability.

sections.heading: Stability under limited feedback.
sections.text: We measure coefficient variability by the mean pairwise ℓ 1 \ell_{1} distance between fits to three feedback subsets, averaged over personas. Tables 14 – 16 report paired differences from bpm . At n = 25 n=25 and 100 100 , posterior means vary less than MLE in all three tasks. Comparisons with regularized estimators depend on the task and budget: RM has lower variability on Summarization at n = 100 n=100 and Story Generation at n = 100,500 n=100,500 , while MAP has lower variability on Story Generation at n = 500 n=500 . Adapted SS differences on Image Captioning remain unresolved beyond n = 10 n=10 . These results support reduced sensitivity relative to MLE under limited feedback, without establishing uniformly minimal coefficient variation.

sections.heading: Coefficient stability and output preference.
sections.text: MLE and adapted SS often yield more preferred outputs than bpm , whereas bpm outperforms RM at both main-table budgets. The posterior mean therefore provides a stable coefficient estimate in the stated settings alongside posterior uncertainty, rather than uniformly maximizing output preference. Coefficient stability does not establish stability of generated behavior: a partial-score diagnostic found higher coefficient variation but slightly lower output-score variation for shrinkage on Summarization at n = 100 n=100 (Supplementary Material, Section S1).

sections.text: We interpolate between MLE and uniform weights, 𝐰 ^ α = ( 1 − α ) ​ 𝐰 ^ MLE + α ​ 𝟏 / L \widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{\alpha}=(1-\alpha)\widehat{\mathbf{w}}_{\mathrm{MLE}}+\alpha\mathbf{1}/L . Table 13 shows task-dependent trade-offs: shrinkage yields more preferred outputs but less stable coefficients on Summarization, while bpm has higher output preference on Image Captioning and Story Generation at n = 100 n=100 . At n = 25 n=25 on the latter two tasks, shrinkage selects uniform weights. This control does not consistently reproduce the posterior mean’s combination of coefficient stability and output preference.

sections.heading: Adapted SS and merge-operator controls.
sections.text: We compare bpm with an adapted Spectral Souping (SS) coefficient estimator ( Chow et al., 2026 ) to examine how their inferred coefficients affect generated outputs. This experiment evaluates the adapted coefficient estimator; Appendix F.2 separately examines coefficient intervals, including those from SS’s sequential Gaussian inference.

sections.heading: F.4 Direct Weighting
sections.text: Given inferred reward weights, bpm uses them directly as coefficients for merging the shared experts. An alternative is to use the same weights to score candidate models and select the one with the highest inferred utility. We examine whether this alternative improves the fitted reward objective and whether it produces outputs that better match persona preferences.

sections.heading: Does direct merging maximize inferred utility?
sections.text: For each fitted 𝐰 ^ \widehat{\mathbf{w}} on Image Captioning , we consider the 21 21 experts, the uniform merge, and twenty random merges. We score their outputs using the inferred utility 𝐰 ^ ⊤ ​ 𝐫 ~ \widehat{\mathbf{w}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{r}} , with the same reward standardization used for that fit. We select the candidate with the highest mean utility on one half of the evaluation inputs, then compare its utility with that of the bpm merge on the other half. This diagnostic measures the inferred reward objective, not preference judgments from the persona. Across seven personas (including Annotator), six budgets ( 10 10 , 25 25 , 50 50 , 100 100 , 250 250 , and 500 500 ), and three feedback draws, selection always returns an individual expert. The selected candidate has higher estimated utility than the bpm merge in 125 125 of 126 126 cells. Thus, directly using inferred reward weights as merge coefficients does not generally maximize the fitted utility over this candidate set. These utility differences alone do not establish which model’s outputs the persona prefers.

sections.heading: Does utility-based selection improve personalization?

The last method serves as a control for whether inferred preferences improve candidate selection. For this experiment, candidates are selected using only the elicitation inputs, without access to evaluation inputs or persona-judge scores. We then evaluate all three methods against the uniform merge on 451 451 Summarization shared test inputs. sections.heading: Personalization gains under supplementary scoring.
sections.text: To assess how conditioning on decided judgments affects the reported personalization gains, we supplement the main win rate with a score that retains valid ties and order-inconsistent comparisons. The central assignment gives these undecided pairs a score of 0.5 0.5 ; bounds account for the unavailable presentation-order decisions. sections.heading: Scoring and aggregation details.
sections.text: We classify verdicts as wins W W , losses L L , ties T T , order-inconsistent comparisons O O , or invalid judgments. The main metric is W / ( W + L ) W/(W+L) . Scoring each presentation order as 1 1 for a win, 0.5 0.5 for a tie, and 0 0 for a loss would assign an order-inconsistent pair 0.25 0.25 , 0.5 0.5 , or 0.75 0.75 , depending on its two decisions. Those decisions were not separately retained in the verdict records. With N = W + L + T + O N=W+L+T+O , we therefore report S c = W + 0.5 ​ T + c ​ O N , c ∈ { 0.25 , 0.5 , 0.75 } , S_{c}=\frac{W+0.5T+cO}{N},\qquad c\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75\}, where S 0.5 S_{0.5} is the central score and the other assignments bound the possible order-inconsistent contributions. This score is a supplementary assignment, not an exact reconstruction of the missing order-level decisions. Invalid judgments are excluded and counted separately; their reported rate is zero throughout the seven-method panel. Scores are computed per persona and feedback draw, then averaged over draws and equally over personas. Confidence intervals use 2,000 shared input-bootstrap resamples, holding feedback draws fixed. Assignment bounds and sampling intervals describe different sources of uncertainty.

Prior work can realize different reward trade-offs by merging reward-specialized experts, given a vector of trade-off weights. In practice, users can more naturally choose between outputs than specify numerical weights. The challenge is therefore to turn these choices into the coefficients required for merging, while accounting for ambiguity when feedback is limited. Our key idea is to treat the unknown reward weights as latent variables: infer a posterior over them from pairwise choices and reward-score differences, and use its mean directly as the merge coefficients. We instantiate this idea as Bayesian Pairwise Merging ( bpm ), whose posterior also characterizes which reward trade-offs remain plausible given the feedback. We evaluate bpm on radiology summarization, image captioning, and story generation, spanning text-to-text and image-to-text generation. With 100 feedback per simulated persona, bpm achieves macro decided win rates of 91.7%, 77.1%, and 64.3% against uniform merge. For six pairs of simulated personas, each prefers the model fitted to its own feedback, a pattern also observed in a human proof-of-concept. In simulations under bpm ’s model and prior, its nominal 90 % 90\% intervals for temperature-scaled reward weights achieve task-averaged marginal coverage of 88.9 % 88.9\% and 89.2 % 89.2\% with only 10 10 and 25 25 comparisons, respectively. bpm thus enables personalization from pairwise feedback without per-user policy training, while characterizing the coefficient ambiguity left by limited feedback. 1 Introduction Personalizing generative models requires adapting to how users trade off competing objectives ( Guan et al., 2025 ; Ji et al., 2026 ) . Existing multi-objective methods can realize different trade-offs once a preference vector is given ( Zhong et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) . A representative example is Rewarded Soups ( Rame et al., 2023 ) , which merges reward-specialized experts with different coefficients to construct models for different preferences. The same expert library can then be reused across users, avoiding a separate training run for every trade-off. These methods assume that the preference weights are already known. Users, however, may find it easier to compare generated outputs than to specify numerical weights over reward dimensions. The central question is how a user’s pairwise choices can supply the missing coefficients for model personalization . Answering this question requires connecting preference inference with model construction. Prior work has shown that pairwise choices can inform estimates of user-specific reward weights ( Bose et al., 2025 ) , but limited feedback may leave multiple weight vectors plausible ( Shenfeld et al., 2025 ) . Yet even accurate reward-weight estimates do not guarantee the intended trade-offs in the merged model ( Rame et al., 2023 , §2.2.3) . Thus, translating uncertain preference estimates into effective merge coefficients remains a challenge. Figure 1: Pairwise feedback personalizes a merged model. Two simulated personas provide different choices (a) , inducing distinct posteriors (b) and merged-model outputs (c) . Each persona favors its corresponding model on shared response pairs (d) . In this work, we propose Bayesian Pairwise Merging ( bpm ) , which connects uncertain preference inference with the construction of a personalized model ( Figure 1 ). To account for the ambiguity left by limited feedback, bpm uses Bayesian inference to obtain a posterior over user-specific reward weights, quantifying the relative support for different trade-offs and the uncertainty that remains. The posterior mean then supplies the coefficients for merging shared reward-specialized experts, enabling classical Bayesian inference to guide the personalization of modern deep generative models without per-user policy training. Our theoretical analysis makes explicit the additional assumptions needed to connect accurate weight estimation with optimality. Experiments on radiology summarization ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , image captioning ( Chen et al., 2015 ) , and story generation ( Fan et al., 2018 ) demonstrate effective personalization and characterize the stability and uncertainty of the inferred coefficients. Our main contributions are threefold. 1. Pairwise feedback supplies effective model-construction coefficients. bpm connects Bayesian reward-weight inference to shared-expert merging, constructing personalized models without explicit user-specified weights or per-user policy training. The inferred coefficients improve on uniform merging across three generation tasks, establishing a practical route from pairwise choices to personalized models (§ 3 and § 5.1 ). 2. Inferred coefficients translate preference differences into model behavior. In simulations under bpm ’s model and prior, compact intervals for temperature-scaled reward weights achieve near-nominal coverage. bpm thus provides reduced coefficient sensitivity and quantified reward-weight ambiguity, complementing output preference as distinct dimensions of personalization (§ 6 , Appendix F ). 2 Related Work Multi-objective alignment with specified preferences. Given a preference vector, existing methods implement the corresponding trade-offs through weighted-reward optimization ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) , preference-conditioned policies ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2024a ) , decoding-time composition ( Shi et al., 2024 ) , or preference-aware model merging ( Rame et al., 2023 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Chen and Kwok, 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Related work on multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrates specialized teachers into a student through additional training ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . bpm addresses how to obtain the preference weights themselves from an individual’s pairwise choices, then uses them to merge shared experts without per-user policy training. Preference inference from pairwise feedback. Prior work learns reward functions from human comparisons ( Christiano et al., 2017 ) and uses Bayesian inference to estimate reward weights as well as their uncertainty ( Biyik and Sadigh, 2018 ; Bıyık et al., 2020 ) . PReF ( Shenfeld et al., 2025 ) and LoRe ( Bose et al., 2025 ) infer user-specific weights over reward components learned across users, while other methods model preference distributions ( Poddar et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . bpm uses predefined reward dimensions without requiring other users’ preference data. In connecting feedback to personalized outputs, UserAlign selects responses from a fixed candidate pool ( Pădurean et al., 2025 ) , while Spectral Souping estimates policy-combination coefficients from online feedback, including through sequential Gaussian posterior updates ( Chow et al., 2026 ) . bpm infers a posterior over reward weights from a fixed offline set of pairwise judgments. 3 Bayesian Pairwise Merging Figure 2: Bayesian Pairwise Merging. Across three generation tasks, the resulting models improve on uniform merging and reflect contrasting simulated persona preferences, while controlled feedback shifts produce corresponding behavioral changes. Gains across expert libraries trained with different optimization methods further support the usefulness of feedback-derived coefficients. Beyond model construction, bpm provides coefficients that vary less than mle across limited-feedback subsets and a posterior quantifying plausible reward weights. In simulations under its model and prior, compact intervals for temperature-scaled reward weights achieve near-nominal coverage. bpm thus connects pairwise feedback to personalized models while making the remaining ambiguity in the inferred preferences explicit.
